name: Mjölnir
powers: Summons thunder and lightning; returns to the thrower's hand; hallows weddings and funerals.
description: The mighty hammer of Thor, forged by the dwarven brothers Brokkr and Sindri as the prize of a wager Loki made on his own head. The hammer's handle came out short because Loki, in fly form, bit the dwarf's hand while he worked the bellows. Mjölnir could shatter mountains, was thrown like a boomerang, and also served to consecrate marriages, births, and funerals. Thor's iron gloves Járngreipr are needed to grip its scorching shaft.

name: Gungnir
powers: Never misses its mark; its throwers and possession pledge a solemn oath.
description: The spear of Odin, forged by the dwarven sons of Ivaldi in a contest against Brokkr and Sindri for Loki's head. The All-Father opened the war between the Æsir and Vanir by hurling Gungnir over the enemy host, an act that became the archetype of casting a spear at the start of a battle. Oaths sworn upon it were considered unbreakable. Odin rides with it at Ragnarök.

name: Draupnir
powers: Drips eight equal rings every ninth night.
description: The gold ring of Odin, forged by Brokkr and Sindri as part of the same wager that produced Mjölnir. Every ninth night, eight rings of equal weight drip from it. When Baldr was laid on his funeral pyre, Odin laid Draupnir on the pyre, but the ring was returned from Hel by Baldr's brother Hermóðr and later burned with Baldr's wife Nanna.

name: Skíðblaðnir
powers: Folds up like a cloth into a pocket; always has a fair wind.
description: The best of all ships, built for Freyr by the dwarven sons of Ivaldi. Large enough to carry all the gods and their weapons, yet it can be folded like a cloth and carried in a pouch when not at sea. It always finds a fair wind wherever it sails. In the Prose Edda, Skíðblaðnir is listed among the treasures the dwarves made for the gods.

name: Brísingamen
powers: Heightens the beauty of its wearer; a treasure of the goddess Freyja.
description: The radiant necklace of the goddess Freyja, forged by the dwarves. In the Prose Edda it is counted among the treasures of the gods; in Lokasenna Loki accuses Freyja of having won it dishonorably from the dwarves. The hero Þórólfr and the god Heimdallr both fight over it in separate sagas, and Heimdallr retrieves it from Loki in the shape of a seal.

name: Gleipnir
powers: Unbreakable binding that holds the wolf Fenrir until Ragnarök.
description: The third and final fetter with which the gods bound the wolf Fenrir, after the chains Lœdingr and Drómi snapped. Forged by the dwarves from six impossible things: the sound of a cat's footfall, a woman's beard, the roots of a mountain, a bear's sinews, a fish's breath, and a bird's spittle. Made as thin as silk, it cannot be broken. The god Týr placed his hand in Fenrir's mouth as a pledge and lost it when the wolf discovered he could not free himself.

name: Andvaranaut
powers: Cursed to bring death and misfortune to every possessor after the dwarf who made it.
description: The ring at the heart of the treasure of the dwarf Andvari, which Loki took from him under the island of the waterfall after catching him in the shape of a pike. Andvari cursed the ring and all the gold, so that it would destroy whoever possessed it. The treasure passed to Hreiðmarr, to the dragon Fáfnir, then to Sigurðr, and brought ruin upon each — a story retold in the Völsunga saga and echoed in the Nibelungenlied.

name: Gram
maker: Reforged by Regin from the shards of Sigmund's blade
powers: Slices through a smith's anvil and the body of the dragon Fáfnir.
description: The sword of the Völsung heroes. Its first owner Sigmund drove it into the Branstock tree, where none but he could pull it out. When the blade broke, the shards were kept and reforged by Regin for Sigmund's son Sigurðr, who proved the blade by splitting the anvil in two and later used it to slay the dragon Fáfnir.

name: Megingjörð
powers: Doubles the god's already godlike strength.
description: The belt of the thunder god Thor which, when he girds it on, doubles his strength. It is named in the Prose Edda alongside his iron gloves Járngreipr as one of the three great possessions of Thor, the third being the hammer Mjölnir. Without it Thor is still mighty; with it, nothing among the giants can stand against him.

name: Járngreipr
powers: Let Thor grip the white-hot shaft of Mjölnir.
description: The iron gauntlets of Thor, one of his three great treasures named in the Prose Edda. Their purpose is practical as much as martial: the handle of Mjölnir grows white-hot in flight, and only the iron gloves allow Thor to grasp the hammer and throw it. The third treasure completes the set — the strength belt Megingjörð.

name: Naglfar
material: Untrimmed fingernails and toenails of the dead
powers: Bear the forces of chaos from the east across the waters at Ragnarök.
description: The great ship of the dead, built from the untrimmed nails and toenails of the dead. The Prose Edda warns that the ship is always under construction, which is why the dead must be buried with clipped nails — trimming the nails of the dead slows its completion. At Ragnarök, Naglfar will sail carrying the fire-giant Surtr's host and the frost giants, steered by the giant Hrym.

name: Hliðskjálf
powers: From it the sitter can see across all the worlds.
description: The high seat of Odin in Valhöll, from which the All-Father can see into all realms and watch over everything that happens among gods, men, and giants. Sitting in Hliðskjálf without leave was dangerous: Freyr sat in it and was struck by the sight of the giantess Gerðr, falling in love with her at a distance. It appears throughout the Eddas as the seat of far-seeing power.

name: Gjallarhorn
powers: Its sound carries across all the worlds; it calls the gods to the final battle.
description: The great horn of Heimdallr, the watchman of the gods, who guards the rainbow bridge Bifröst. In the Prose Edda, Heimdallr drinks from it at the well and will blow it when the world ends; at Ragnarök the horn's blast is heard throughout the worlds, summoning gods and men to the final battle. It may double as a drinking vessel in some accounts.

name: Hringhorni
powers: The greatest of ships, large enough to bear a god's funeral pyre.
description: The greatest of all ships, in which the gods laid the body of Baldr upon a funeral pyre after his death by the mistletoe spear. The launching of Hringhorni was so heavy that only the giantess Hyrrokkin could push it into the sea. It appears in the Prose Edda's account of Baldr's funeral and in some skaldic references.

name: Ægishjálmr
powers: Strikes fear into enemies and grants the wearer protection in battle.
description: The Helm of Awe, an Icelandic magical stave drawn as a cross with branching prongs. In the Eddas it is the treasure of Fáfnir the dragon, which made its bearer invincible; in later Icelandic grimoires (galdrabækur) it was drawn on the forehead between the brows to terrify opponents and grant victory. Modern folk practice still reproduces it as a protective sign.

name: Vegvísir
powers: Guides the bearer safely through storms and unknown lands.
description: The Wayfinder, an Icelandic magical stave drawn as a central point with radiating runic spokes, attested in the Huld manuscript (1860). The accompanying charm promises that whoever bears it will never lose their way in storm or bad weather, even when the way is unknown. It has become a widely reproduced symbol of Icelandic folk magic in modern culture.

name: Gallehus Golden Horns
maker: Maker named in runic inscription: LagestheR
powers: Ceremonial drinking and ritual horns; images thought to invoke protection and fertility.
description: Two golden horns of the 5th century, found at Gallehus in southern Jutland in 1639 and 1734 and stolen and melted down in 1802. The longer horn bore a runic inscription naming its maker, LagestheR. The horns' densely decorated bands of men, beasts, and symbols have been read as ritual or cultic imagery. Reconstructions are held in Copenhagen; they remain among the most famous objects of Nordic antiquity.

name: The Sunken Church Bell
powers: Said to ring from beneath the water on holy nights, and to be recoverable only by one pure of heart.
description: A recurring Swedish folk motif: a church bell lost in a lake — swept overboard while being ferried, or dragged down by the water folk (or a troll) because its ringing disturbed them. The bell is said to toll faintly beneath the surface on Christmas night or other holy nights, and treasure-hunters who try to raise it with a pure heart may catch a glimpse of it before it slips away. Variants are told across Sweden, Norway, and Finland.

name: Troll's Gift Ring
powers: Gifts from the hidden folk bring luck to those who accept them without greed, and ruin to the grasping.
description: In Norwegian and Scandinavian folk belief, the hulder and the troll folk sometimes press gifts upon humans — rings, bracelets, or coins that look like gold. Accepting such a gift courteously could bring lasting luck, while greedily taking more, or refusing rudely, brought misfortune. The motif is widely told across Norway, Sweden, and Denmark, with many local variations on what the gift becomes at dawn.
source: Norwegian folk tradition (eventyr and sagn collections)

name: Sampo
powers: Grinds out grain, salt, and gold for its possessor.
description: The wonder-working mill of Finnish epic, forged by the smith Ilmarinen as the price for the hand of the maiden of Pohjola. The Sampo ground out limitless grain, salt, and gold, making its possessor rich. In the Kalevala, the heroes of Väinölä and the mistress of Pohjola fight over it; in the battle the Sampo is smashed and lost at sea, and its fragments grant the sea its richness. Its shape and true nature are never fully described.

name: Tyrfing
aliases: The Cursed Sword of Hervarar saga
powers: Never misses and never rusts, but kills a man every time it is drawn and brings three great evils.
description: Cursed sword of the Hervarar saga, forged by the dwarves Dvalinn and Dulinn for King Svafrlami, whom they cursed in return: the blade would kill a man each time it was drawn, never rust, and bring about three great evils. Hervör raised it from the barrow of her dead father Angantýr, and the curse worked ruin on every bearer after.

name: Óðrœrir
aliases: The Kettle of the Mead of Poetry
powers: Holds the mead of poetry; whoever drinks it gains poetry and wisdom.
description: The kettle that holds the mead of poetry, brewed by the dwarves Fjalar and Galar from the blood of Kvasir, the wisest of beings, mixed with honey. Whoever drinks from Óðrœrir gains the gift of poetry and wisdom. Odin stole the mead from the giant Suttungr, drained the vessels Boðn and Són and the kettle itself, and shared it with the Æsir, keeping a small part for poets.

name: Sif's Golden Hair
aliases: The Gold of the Sons of Ivaldi
powers: Grows from the head like real hair and never loses its gleam.
description: The golden hair of Sif, wife of Thor, wrought by the dwarven sons of Ivaldi after Loki maliciously cut off her own. Made of gold so fine that it grew from her head like real hair, it became proof of the dwarves' skill and opened the great contest of gifts between rival smiths. Loki commissioned it to atone for his mischief, and Thor kept his skull intact.

name: Gullinbursti
powers: Its golden bristles light the darkest night, and it runs through air and water faster than any horse.
description: Freyr's golden boar, forged by the dwarves Brokkr and Sindri during the same wager that produced Mjölnir. Its bristles shone so brightly that they lit the dark, and it could run through air and water alike. Odin judged it the finest of the dwarves' treasures, and Snorri records it as fit to draw Freyr's chariot in place of a horse.

name: Freyr's Sword
aliases: The Sword That Fights by Itself
powers: Fights of its own accord, without a hand to wield it.
description: The self-fighting sword of Freyr, which he gave to his servant Skírnir as payment for wooing the giantess Gerðr on his behalf. Stripped of his blade, Freyr was weaponless when the fire giant Surtr faced him at Ragnarök, and he fell. The sword is remembered in the Eddas as the price of love and the cause of a god's death.

name: Víðarr's Shoe
aliases: The Shoe of the Silent God
material: Scrap leather gathered from all men's shoes
powers: Holds firm against Fenrir's jaws so Víðarr can tear the wolf apart at Ragnarök.
description: The shoe of Víðarr, son of Odin, made from the pieces of leather that people cut from their own shoes at toe and heel and set aside for the god. At Ragnarök the silent Víðarr set the shoe against Fenrir's lower jaw, gripped the wolf's upper jaw with his hands, and tore his mouth open, avenging his father Odin.

name: Drómi and Leyding
powers: Failed bindings; only the silken dwarf-made fetter Gleipnir finally held Fenrir.
description: The two fetters with which the gods first tried to bind the wolf Fenrir. The first, Leyding, the wolf snapped as easily as if it were a cord. The stronger Drómi held him briefly until he braced his feet against the ground and shattered it, sending the fragments flying. Only the silken dwarf-made fetter Gleipnir was strong enough to hold him until Ragnarök.

name: Svalinn
powers: Tempering the sun's rays so the earth and sea are not consumed by fire.
description: The shield that stands before the sun, named in Grímnismál, sheltering earth and sea from the burning rays of the sun goddess Sól. The poem warns that if the shield ever falls away, mountains and the deep sea would be consumed by flame. It is one of the most purely cosmic objects in the Eddic corpus, a world-sustaining object rather than a warrior's arm.

name: Hǫfuð
powers: The sword of Heimdall, watchman of the gods, named among his possessions in the Edda.
description: Hǫfuð, 'Head', the sword of Heimdall, watchman of the gods, named among his possessions in Gylfaginning. Snorri lists the blade beside Heimdall's role as guardian of the gods, and later tradition links it to the final battle, where Heimdall and Loki are said to slay each other at Ragnarök. It is one of the few named Eddic swords with no surviving owner story.

name: Lævateinn
maker: Unnamed (forged with rune magic in some readings)
powers: The only weapon said able to slay the rooster Viðófnir at the top of the world tree.
description: The 'wounding wand' of Fjölsvinnsmál, the blade with which alone the rooster Viðófnir, perched at the top of the world tree, could be slain. It lies in a chest beside the giantess Sinmara, bound by nine locks that only a feather plucked from Viðófnir's own tail can open. Scholars debate whether it is Loki's sword or a separate weapon; its name may itself be a late emendation.

name: Gríðarvölr
powers: A staff of might lent to Thor, with which he slew the giant Geirröðr.
description: The staff of the giantess Gríðr, lent by her to Thor along with iron gloves and a belt of might when he set out against the giant Geirröðr. With the staff in hand Thor broke Geirröðr's back and killed him. The loan, told in Skáldskaparmál, is a rare act of kindness by a giantess toward the thunder god.

name: Freyja's Falcon Cloak
powers: Lets its wearer fly in the shape of a falcon.
description: The falcon cloak of the goddess Freyja, a feather garment that lets its wearer fly in the shape of a falcon. Loki borrows it to fetch the goddess Iðunn back from the giant Þjazi, and later to pursue the giant in the same form. In the Prose Edda the cloak is the gods' regular means of swift flight, kept in Freyja's keeping.

name: Nábrók
maker: Made by the wearer from a dead man's lower body
powers: Said to keep the wearer's purse from ever running empty.
description: Nábrók, the 'necropants' of Icelandic folk magic: trousers stitched from the skin cut from the lower body of a dead man, worn by the living. The wearer kept a coin in the pants that was said always to return to his purse, keeping him wealthy as long as the grisly garment lasted. The custom is documented in Icelandic folklore as a means of conjuring luck, not a mythic heirloom.

name: Draumstafir
powers: Drawn so the sleeper receives good or revealing dreams.
description: Draumstafir, the dream stave of the Huld manuscript, a complex magical sign drawn so that the sleeper receives good or revealing dreams. It is one of the many galdrastafir recorded by 19th-century collectors of Icelandic folk magic, and the sign is still reproduced in books and tattoos, though the drawing instructions vary between grimoires.

name: Kaupaloki
powers: Brings success and fair fortune in buying and selling.
description: Kaupaloki, the trade-luck stave of the Huld manuscript, inscribed for success in buying and selling. Drawn or carved by merchants, it was meant to bring profit and good dealings in the market. It belongs to the practical folk magic of Iceland's seafaring trade, where a stave for fair fortune in commerce was worth its weight in cargo.

name: Pungastafur
powers: Keeps the bearer's purse heavy and money from running short.
description: Pungastafur, the purse stave of the Huld manuscript, drawn so that money would not run short and the bearer's purse would stay heavy. It belongs to the family of luck-and-money galdrastafir and was among the most sought-after signs in the grimoire tradition, a domestic charm against poverty in a subsistence economy.

name: Smjörstafur
powers: Brings success in making butter.
description: Smjörstafur, the butter stave of the Huld manuscript, drawn or carved to bring success in butter-making. In an agrarian world where dairy was wealth, a charm for a full churn was practical magic, and the stave sits among the agricultural signs recorded beside the luck and protection staves of the grimoires.

name: Þjófastafur
powers: Protects livestock and goods from thieves.
description: Þjófastafur, the thief stave of the Huld manuscript, drawn to guard livestock and goods against theft. The name means 'thief-stave', and the sign was meant to make a thief unable to take what belonged to the bearer. It answered a real fear in the farmsteads, protecting herds and households that had no other defence.

name: Óttastafur
powers: Strikes fear into those against whom it is used.
description: Óttastafur, the fear stave of the Huld manuscript, drawn to strike fear into others. As a weapon of psychological magic it was meant to cow rivals or enemies without a blow. It is one of the aggressive galdrastafir recorded beside the protective and luck-giving signs, showing that the stave tradition served harm as readily as help.

name: Bjargástafur
powers: Carries the bearer through danger and hardship unharmed.
description: Bjargástafur, the rescue stave of the Huld manuscript, drawn so that the bearer could escape or survive any danger. Its name derives from bjarga, 'to save', and the grimoire tradition promises that no misfortune could hold a person who bore it. It is one of the general talismans of protection in Icelandic folk magic.

name: Ginfaxi
powers: Turns the luck of a rival or competitor, so the bearer wins the contest.
description: Ginfaxi, the rival-beating stave of the Huld manuscript, drawn to defeat an opponent in competition or argument. Its name echoes the animal names of Norse myth, but here it belongs to a sign meant to turn luck against rivals. It is one of the combative staves of Icelandic folk magic, used when the prize was trade, a case, or a contest.
